title: On the way
hookLine: the commute can be a pilgrimage
tomorrow: can wiping trays at 6 a.m. count as anything holy?

lines: A BLIND MAN STARTS TO SHOUT.
cards: The 5:40 bus, still dark. Hoods up, earbuds in, every face lit by the same small screen. Nobody on this ride would call it a journey, least of all the driver.

It's the dead part of the day, between home and work. Mark tells about a road like that, the busy one out of Jericho, crowded with travelers. Jesus is on it, going up toward Jerusalem with his disciples and a big crowd.
At the side of the road sits a blind man named Bartimaeus. He hears the crowd go by, and he starts to shout.

teach.b: The crowd tells him to be quiet. He shouts louder: son of David, have mercy on me. And here is the turn.
The whole procession, on its way up to the holy city, stands still for one man at the edge of the road.
Jesus has him called over and asks a question that sounds almost too simple, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "What wilt thou that I should do to thee?" Bartimaeus asks to see.
Mark ends the scene like this: "And immediately he saw, and followed him in the way." In the way. The same road, the same crowd, the same trip, with one more person on it who can now see.
A pilgrimage, in Catholic practice, is a journey made as a prayer: the walking is part of it, not just the getting there. A commute can be that too.

teach.h: THE ROUTE STAYS; THE NOTICING CHANGES.
teach.b: The route doesn't change. What changes is who you notice on it.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight.
The Catechism says the Jesus Prayer, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners, joins a hymn from Paul with the cry of the tax collector and of the blind men begging for light.
A shout from the roadside became a prayer people still pray.

how: Catholics make pilgrimages to shrines and holy places, praying along the road; some keep the same habit on an ordinary commute, praying for the people they pass.

o: the road to work, walked like a pilgrimage
the long road to heaven after a person dies
a Lenten walk that stops at fourteen crosses

games.q: who's on the road — tap the pairs.

s: the healing happens once Jesus reaches Jerusalem
it happens on the road out of Jericho, on the way up.
the Catechism links the Jesus Prayer to blind men begging for light
it joins their cry with the tax collector's and a hymn from Paul.
a pilgrimage only counts once you reach the shrine
in Catholic practice the walking is part of the prayer, and Mark's story happens on the way.

games.q: on your bus, a man keeps asking people for change and the driver tells him to sit down. by Mark's road, what comes first?
o: look at him, actually see him; that's where the story starts.
look away; the driver has it handled.
change seats so the ride stays calm for everyone.
games.why: the crowd told Bartimaeus to hush. Jesus stood still and called him over. noticing comes first; what you do next is yours to choose.

practice: Bring to mind the route you take most days, stop by stop: the corner, the crossing, the person who's always at the same bus shelter.
As each face comes up, give it one silent line, the Kyrie from Mass, Lord, have mercy, or simply a good wish. Keep going down the route until the bell.

wordCard.voice: On the way. The road between home and work, walked like a pilgrimage, the way Bartimaeus followed in the way.

orig.note: Greek: in the way, on the road. Mark's last words about Bartimaeus.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a daily pilgrimage, the same road with your eyes up. See you tomorrow.
